inline.s: Those who do not understand the principle clearly are not being said to have no view at all. But once they take a single view to be the highest and are thereby obscured by that one view, then what was high is no longer high. Consider the five eyes: the Buddha-eye is naturally taken to be the highest, yet people fail to see that it is precisely because each of the other four eyes is distinctly supreme that it is called the Buddha-eye. This is why the Tathāgata clings to no single view and perfectly possesses all five eyes; those who cling to one view should understand this. Those who consider themselves right are likewise not being said to be wholly wrong. But if they insist on holding up their own rightness alone and will not agree with the views of others, then what was right is no longer right. Consider the sands of the Ganges: spoken of in terms of nature they are certainly not so, yet spoken of in terms of marks, why should they not be so? Marks are the marks of nature itself; why must one discard marks in order to make nature clear? This is why the Tathāgata clings to no divergent view and speaks of those sands; those who cling to divergent views should understand this. In sum, whoever clings to a view thereby establishes something. Hence, whether oneness or difference, if one does not lean to this side one leans to that. This comes about through attachment to a self. Now the teaching is that neither oneness nor difference may be clung to; where then can a view be established? Then the self too is transformed along with it. Is this not the sword of wisdom that cuts off the self?

The meaning of neither one nor different is the essential doctrine of prajñā and the vital principle of the Buddhadharma; it can penetrate all dharmas. Therefore this sutra has those who understand the dharma of no-self first understand this. Expanded, this phrase yields the eight negations, the ten negations, the twelve negations, and the fourteen negations. Thus the Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom says: “Neither arising nor ceasing, neither annihilated nor eternal, neither one nor different, neither going nor coming; dharmas born of causes and conditions put an end to all idle speculation.” Dharmas born of causes and conditions is another way of saying that all dharmas arise from conditions, and also another way of saying cause and effect. For dharmas born of causes and conditions are the dharmas produced by causes and conditions, and dharmas are the fruits born of causes. Hence dharmas born of causes and conditions, put briefly, is simply cause and effect. This says that all dharmas are cause and effect, and therefore all dharmas are neither arising nor ceasing, neither annihilated nor eternal, neither one nor different, neither going nor coming. This is what is meant by the eight negations. If one does not understand the meaning of the eight negations, one does not understand cause and effect, and then everything one says becomes idle speculation. This precisely reveals that the meaning of the eight negations and of cause and effect is right discourse and right view. Dharmas that arise from conditions are precisely arising and ceasing; how can they be called neither arising nor ceasing? One does not understand that when conditions gather they arise and when conditions disperse they cease, and that this is spoken in terms of the marks of dharmas. Seeing the arising and ceasing of the marks of dharmas is enough to prove that the nature of dharmas is fundamentally neither arising nor ceasing. Neither going nor coming is likewise spoken in terms of the nature of dharmas. Cause upon cause and fruit upon fruit never cease, hence neither annihilated. A cause completes a fruit, and the fruit again becomes a cause, hence neither eternal. All dharmas each have their own cause and effect, hence neither one. All dharmas do not go beyond cause and effect, hence neither different. If the meaning of the eight negations were developed exclusively in terms of cause and effect, it could fill a whole book; here I only speak of it briefly.

The Treatise on Wisdom also says: “Contemplate all dharmas as neither arising nor ceasing, neither increasing nor decreasing, neither defiled nor pure, neither coming nor going, neither one nor different, neither eternal nor annihilated, neither existent nor non-existent.” This states the fourteen negations. If the phrase neither existent nor non-existent is taken as explaining the meaning of the six phrases from neither arising nor ceasing onward, then they become the twelve negations. The Madhyamaka Treatise also sets out the eight negations: “Neither arising nor ceasing, neither eternal nor annihilated, neither one nor different, neither coming nor going forth; able to speak of causes and conditions, it well extinguishes all idle speculation.” Going forth means the same as going. Both treatises were composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna to make prajñā clear. Master Jiazang’s Great Treatise on the Mahāyāna says: “The eight negations are the heart of all Buddhas, the ground of practice of all sages. Vertically they pierce all sutras; horizontally they pervade all treatises.” And his Commentary on the Madhyamaka Treatise says: “They are the home of right contemplation, the very marrow of the Vaipulya teachings. They settle what is partial and what is correct in the Buddhadharma and reveal the root and source of gain and loss. Deluded about them, the eighty thousand treasuries of Dharma are as dark as traveling by night; awakened to them, the twelve divisions of scripture are like facing the white sun.” Truly, such phrases and meanings are precisely what opens people’s Buddha-knowledge and Buddha-vision and removes the deluded thoughts and false reckonings they have always clung to. Everything the Buddha spoke makes this meaning clear: what is called the ultimate meaning, the supreme meaning, the Middle Way. If this meaning is not understood, the essential purport of the Buddhadharma is not clear, and how could one cultivate and realize perfectly? Hence it is said to be the heart of all Buddhas and the ground of practice of all sages; deluded about it, one travels by night, awakened to it, one sees the white sun.

Yet Nāgārjuna in fact based himself on such sutras as the Original Karma and the Necklace, though the order differs slightly. That sutra says: “The meaning of the two truths is neither one nor two, neither eternal nor annihilated, neither coming nor going, neither arising nor ceasing.” Neither two means not different. The two truths are the ultimate truth, which speaks of the nature of dharmas, and the conventional truth, which speaks of the marks of dharmas. The sutra uses the eight negations to clarify the two truths, while the treatise uses the eight negations to clarify arising from conditions, because this meaning pervades all dharmas. The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra sets out the ten negations: “The twelve links of conditioned co-arising: neither going forth nor ceasing, neither eternal nor annihilated, neither one nor two, neither coming nor going, neither cause nor fruit.” Neither going forth nor ceasing means neither arising nor ceasing; neither one nor two means neither one nor different.

Neither cause nor fruit does not mean that cause and effect do not exist. The first phrase speaks of the twelve links of conditioned co-arising, meaning that dharmas born of the twelve links do not go beyond the meaning of these ten negations; dharmas born of causes and conditions precisely make cause and effect clear. It means that spoken of in terms of cause and effect, what is called a cause is itself the fruit of a preceding cause, and what is called a fruit is itself the cause of a succeeding fruit. This makes clear that cause and effect are inexhaustible, and one must not cling to the idea that a cause is fixedly a cause or a fruit fixedly a fruit. Hence it is said to be neither cause nor fruit. Further, speaking of nature and marks together, spoken of in terms of the nature of cause and effect, they are darkly one in a single flavor, and one cannot say who is cause and who is fruit; but spoken of in terms of the marks of cause and effect, the facts are clearly distinguished, cause is cause and fruit is fruit, a cause must have its fruit and a fruit must have its cause. Yet just when they are clearly distinguished, they are darkly one in a single flavor. Why? Because marks are not apart from nature. And just when they are darkly one in a single flavor, they are perfectly distinct. Why? Because nature is not apart from marks. This is what is meant by neither cause nor fruit. This joins with the first phrase to make the meaning clear; this is why this sutra says “is not” and then says “is named.” This is why one should not grasp dharmas and should not grasp non-dharmas, and should cling neither to emptiness nor to existence. This is why the Madhyamaka Treatise says: “Dharmas born of causes and conditions, I say, are emptiness; they are also called provisional names, and also called the Middle Way.” It means that one who wishes to know that all dharmas do not go beyond cause and effect should understand the meaning of being at once empty and provisional. If one does not understand that emptiness is precisely the provisional, one falls into the view of annihilation, all things come to nothing, and one denies cause and effect. If one does not understand that the provisional is precisely emptiness, one falls into the view of eternity, all things seem fixed, and one likewise denies cause and effect. One should know that although we speak of emptiness and the provisional, in truth emptiness and the provisional are neither one nor different. Understanding this meaning is the Middle Way; there is no separate Middle Way outside emptiness and the provisional. Emptiness is the nature of dharmas, the ultimate truth; the provisional is the marks of dharmas, the conventional truth. The section on the five eyes here makes clear the ultimate truth of the nature of dharmas; the nature of dharmas is originally thus and all is so, so why cling to oneness? The section on the river sands makes clear the conventional truth of the marks of dharmas; the marks of dharmas are originally accordant with conditions and without fixity, so why cling to difference? The eight negations, ten negations, twelve negations and so on are merely different ways of opening and combining; if opened out in detail they could reach to immeasurable phrases, and if condensed to the utmost, neither one nor different embraces them all. Therefore the opening of the Buddha’s perfect vision here clarifies the meaning solely in terms of neither one nor different.

Now let me speak briefly again of the meaning of the eight negations, and why it penetrates the principle of all sutras and treatises. One should know that what the Buddha taught does not go beyond the two truths, ultimate and conventional. The marks of dharmas under the conventional truth, though they change and are impermanent, are seen in common by the worldly, and so are called conventional. The nature of dharmas under the ultimate truth is constant and unchanging and is the essence of all dharmas, and so is called ultimate. The Buddha taught the two truths and used the meaning of the eight negations to explain them both. They are called truths because they make clear that the fact and the principle are truly not false. The reason all living beings revolve in the bitter realms of birth and death without bound is nothing else: it is because they are deluded about the meaning of the eight negations of the conventional truth. The reason all hearers and even bodhisattvas at the stage of expedient devices have transformation birth and death and have not exhausted ignorance is nothing else: it is because they are deluded about the meaning of the eight negations of the ultimate truth. In sum, simply because of these eight negations, delusion has its depths and awakening its heights, and so there is the profusion of the six paths and the distinctions among the three vehicles. The Buddha appeared in the world for one great matter, namely to lead living beings to escape the two kinds of birth and death. Therefore he taught various dharmas to reveal and show them, so that they might awaken and enter. And those various dharmas do not go beyond the meaning of the eight negations of the two truths, ultimate and conventional. Hence this meaning penetrates all sutras and treatises.

The word “not” has two meanings. First, the meaning of breaking, breaking one’s clinging to all marks. Second, the meaning of dissolving, dissolving marks to reveal nature. But breaking has two meanings: it breaks not only clinging to existence but also clinging to emptiness. Dissolving likewise has two meanings: it not only dissolves marks to reveal nature but also dissolves nature to reveal marks, so as to bring about perfect interfusion.

Let me now take the phrase neither arising nor ceasing and set out its essentials, using the phrase neither one nor different to pervade it. First, in terms of the conventional truth. Worldly people all cling to the idea that there is real arising and real ceasing. The Buddha tells them that none of it is real: only because causes and conditions gather does a mark of arising falsely appear, and when causes and conditions disperse a mark of ceasing falsely appears. Your own nature has never arisen or ceased. But you merely cling to marks and are blind to nature; that is why you have the misery of revolving in birth and death. This clarifies the Middle Way in terms of the conventional truth. When the Middle Way is clear, it is no longer the conventional truth but the ultimate truth. This is how the sickness of clinging to existence is cured.

Next, in terms of the ultimate truth. The sages of the two vehicles and bodhisattvas at the stage of expedient devices in turn cling to neither arising nor ceasing. The Buddha tells them: neither arising nor ceasing is meant to cure ordinary beings’ clinging to the marks of arising and ceasing. How can one remove one clinging and give rise to another? You should know that nature and marks are not two, and emptiness and existence are simultaneous. Existence is precisely emptiness, so the arising and ceasing of the conventional truth is false arising and false ceasing. Emptiness is precisely existence, so the neither arising nor ceasing of the ultimate truth is likewise false non-arising and false non-ceasing. Since you have seen the nature, you should manifest marks and, according with conditions, save living beings. Moreover, the nature is fundamentally not apart from marks, yet you merely cling to nature and weary of marks; that is why you have the misery of transformation birth and death. This clarifies the Middle Way in terms of the ultimate truth. When the Middle Way is clear, it is the supreme vehicle, the one Buddha vehicle. This is how the sickness of clinging to emptiness is cured.

To pervade this with neither one nor different: where the conventional truth clings to arising and ceasing, then arising and ceasing are not one; where one does not cling and is neither arising nor ceasing, then arising and ceasing are not different. Where the ultimate truth clings to neither arising nor ceasing, then neither arising nor ceasing and arising and ceasing are not one; where one does not cling and nature and marks are not two and emptiness and existence are simultaneous, then arising and ceasing and neither arising nor ceasing are not different. For since emptiness and existence are simultaneous, then at the very time of neither arising nor ceasing there is no harm in manifesting arising and ceasing; and though arising and ceasing are manifested, it is still neither arising nor ceasing. This is what is meant by dwelling in neither birth and death nor nirvāṇa. Then oneness and difference alike cannot be spoken of, and even the name neither one nor different is dissolved along with them. Seen in this way, one may know that nothing whatsoever can be clung to, nor is there any need to cling. Therefore the phrases of the eight negations are the wondrous meaning that transforms and removes clinging views, and the meaning of neither one nor different can pervade all those phrases.

All these phrases and meanings reveal that every dharma is thus. Every dharma being thus is the perfect interfusion of the Middle Way, the ultimate meaning. Hence the phrases of the eight negations are also the perfect interfusion of the Middle Way, the ultimate meaning; only the flavor of the Dharma differs. Why is this said? Every dharma being thus is a perfect revelation, what is called a positive exposition; the Tiantai and Huayan schools established themselves on this meaning. The phrases of the eight negations are the essential doctrine of prajñā, which reveals by way of dispelling, what is called a negative exposition; the Three Treatises school established itself on this meaning. The Chan school too follows prajñā’s dispelling and sweeping away, though it does not expound doctrine. One should know that one must first dispel and sweep away before perfect interfusion can be revealed. Thus in this sutra, only after transcending marks and transcending thoughts is it said that every dharma is thus. The Buddha’s intent can be seen. Why? If clinging views are not dispelled, how can there be perfect interfusion? And to cling to perfect interfusion is itself not perfect interfusion. This is why the Awakening of Faith makes clear that non-emptiness must come forth from emptiness. Those who establish the perfect school and teach its perfect meaning are not thereby failing to teach the meaning of dispelling and sweeping away; but even when they teach dispelling and sweeping away, it carries the flavor of perfection. Those who follow dispelling and sweeping away, such as the Three Treatises school, are likewise not failing to teach the meaning of perfect interfusion; but even when they teach perfect interfusion, it carries the flavor of dispelling and sweeping away. Thus their words are like a keen knife and a sharp axe, leaving nothing unbroken, and reading them is like cold water poured down the back, stirring a person to deep reflection. Sadly, since the teachings of prajñā became unclear in the world, even the Treatise on Wisdom and the books of the Three Treatises school have rarely been inquired into. Hence from the Sui and Tang dynasties onward it was only in Chan that the most people of caliber emerged. The reason for this is worth long and deep reflection. One should know that if students do not earnestly work at dispelling and sweeping away but merely memorize countless perfect meanings, how can they break through their emotional clinging? And if emotional clinging is not removed, how can they reach perfect interfusion? This sutra says: All Buddhas and the dharmas of all Buddhas’ supreme, perfect enlightenment all come forth from this sutra. This precisely and directly points to prajñā as the essential gate for entering the Buddha’s path and the stairway to sagehood. This matter concerns the flourishing or decline of the Dharma-gate and the success or failure of students, and is of the utmost importance. Therefore I cannot but speak of it again and again with keen urgency.

Since the Three Treatises school takes prajñā as its doctrine, those who study prajñā cannot but apply their minds to the books of the Three Treatises. Even if one cannot read them all, one must read one or two of them to taste the flavor of the Dharma, so that the great purport of prajñā is easier to grasp. Works such as the Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom, the Great Treatise on the Mahāyāna, and the Commentary on the Madhyamaka Treatise are the best at breaking people’s stubborn clinging and opening the gate of their awakening. But since their meaning is profound and their language abstruse, one must only read them repeatedly and quietly receive them, so as to investigate them. Even so, to say that investigating the works listed above gives one a thorough understanding of the meaning and purport of prajñā would again be mistaken. One should know that the meanings of the eight negations are merely the essential doctrine of prajñā. The winding and subtle depths within prajñā cannot be clearly understood unless one truly investigates and truly examines them from the place of transcending marks and transcending thoughts. This principle too must not go unknown. For the great outline is not different, while the subtleties are not one. Nor is this all. Even comparing the prajñā taught in the former eight assemblies and the latter seven assemblies with this sutra, the same holds: the essential doctrine and great purport are not different from one another, while the subtle flavors of meaning are not one with one another. Thus one sutra has one sutra’s essential doctrine and one sutra’s manner of speaking; how could one penetration make all penetrate? One should know that what the Buddha speaks is the Buddha’s realm. What is called the true mark of all dharmas can be fully known only by a Buddha with a Buddha; even the great bodhisattvas have not fully known it, let alone ordinary beings. That is why the fifty-three good teachers visited by Sudhana at the Huayan assembly all said, “I know only this Dharma-gate; of others I do not know.” These were true words, not modest phrases. That is why ancient worthies such as Zhiyi, Jiazang, and Xianshou spent their lives expounding only a few sutras and treatises; their learning could reach no further. This is precisely the loftiness and the truthfulness of the ancient worthies, which later students should strive to emulate. Nor is it only the phrases of the eight negations in the Three Treatises that can clarify only the essentials of prajñā; the subtle purport still lies in the student’s own receiving. Even if someone today were to write books and establish doctrines setting out the meaning of this sutra and proclaiming it point by point, obtaining such a book would only add one more aid; it would still lie in the student’s own receiving. Why? Even if that person had already become a bodhisattva, the Buddha’s realm could still not be fully known. Even if he were suddenly enlightened as a Buddha and could proclaim it thoroughly, a reader whose obstructions are not yet removed would still not be able to understand it thoroughly. One must still truly investigate and truly examine from the place of transcending marks and transcending thoughts, and only then can one enter. Just so, the meaning made clear in these two sections on clinging neither to oneness nor to difference must, once heard, be used as this Dharma-seal to be minutely confirmed against all dharmas; still more must this Dharma-seal be confirmed against one’s own mind and against the place before a single thought arises. In this way one may hope for penetration. If one merely hears the meaning of these two sections and understands it, that can only be called understanding, not penetration. This principle above all must not go unknown. Penetration means reaching in all four directions and eight reaches without the slightest obstruction. Therefore if in one’s own mind and in all dharmas one’s practice meets with the slightest obstruction, it is not penetration. Below, right knowledge is made clear; it sets out a model for students to follow, so that with the standpoint of neither one nor different they may know the why and wherefore of the mind’s activity and of all dharmas, and thereby seek penetration and no-self.
(Yin) Next, making clear right knowledge. This has two parts: (Mao) first, making clear that the mind’s activity cannot be grasped; next, making clear that all dharmas arise from conditions.

The mind’s activity means the movement of the mind, that is, the arising of a single thought. All dharmas means outer objects. Clarifying right knowledge in terms of inner mind and outer objects is intended to make one know that there is no object and only consciousness, and that outside the mind there are no dharmas. Since outside the mind there are no dharmas, no dharma goes beyond the one true suchness. But living beings are deluded outwardly by the marks of objects and disturbed inwardly by thoughts, and so cannot realize it. This is why prajñā has one transcend marks and transcend thoughts. Cannot be grasped means cannot be obtained. The essence of the nature is empty and still and fundamentally has no thought, and so it is said to be unobtainable. All dharmas are nothing but the gathering of conditions falsely manifesting a mark of arising; they are fundamentally unborn, and this is what is meant by being empty in their very substance. Therefore spoken of in terms of the mind’s activity and all dharmas, they are not one; and spoken of in terms of being unobtainable and arising from conditions, they are not different. Neither one nor different is the meaning of the thusness of all dharmas, and one should know it in this way. Knowing it in this way is called right knowledge because it is the knowing of one who knows in accordance with what the supreme, perfect enlightenment itself has realized and knows. Knowing this, one knows the why and wherefore of transcending thoughts and transcending marks. Transcending marks and transcending thoughts is precisely what makes no-self possible.

(Mao) First, making clear that the mind’s activity cannot be grasped. This has three parts: (Chen) first, a simile to make the assembly understand; next, an explanation that it is not mind; third, a summary that it cannot be grasped. (Chen) The first again has two: (Ji) first, citing the simile; next, knowing them all.
(Ji) First, citing the simile.

["Subhūti, what do you think? Suppose there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in one Ganges River, and suppose the Buddha-worlds were as numerous as all the grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers; would that not be many?" "Very many, World-Honored One."]

In the popular editions there is a “sand” after “such” in “there are such,” while the ancient editions do not have it and it may be omitted. About to make right knowledge clear, the text takes up the discussion of river sands from the perfect vision above as an introduction, meaning to show that the meaning to be clarified below cannot be understood by ordinary sentiments and worldly views that cling to oneness or difference. One must first open one’s perfect vision and cling to neither oneness nor difference before this right knowledge can be opened. It also shows that what is said below should be pervaded by the meaning of neither one nor different. About to speak of living beings’ deluded minds and of all dharmas, the text must first set up a simile, using sand to figure the river and then figuring the sand within the river; this means to show that the deluded mind and all dharmas arise layer upon layer, drawing in ever more and more, beyond counting. It also shows that the marks of the deluded mind and of dharmas are like an illusion and like a transformation, nothing but false existence. All of this is intimate, pointed language; to regard it as unimportant and a mere redundancy would be to betray the sutra text.

In opening with the words “what do you think,” the Buddha, about to open their right knowledge, first tests their standpoint. The intent runs straight through to “cannot be obtained”; it is not merely asking whether it is many. The word “suppose” shows that this is figurative language. The sand in one Ganges River is already beyond counting. “There were as many” refers to that countless sand; it means to suppose that the number of Ganges Rivers equaled the grains of sand in one Ganges River, which is to say countless Ganges Rivers. “All those Ganges Rivers” refers to those countless Ganges Rivers in the previous phrase, and speaks of all the sand in those countless Ganges Rivers. How could their number be measured? Buddha-worlds means great chiliocosms. Each great chiliocosm is the region taught and transformed by one Buddha, and so is called a Buddha-world. “Suppose” refers to the immeasurable spoken of in the previous phrase and means immeasurable worlds. “Would that not be many?” asks whether this can be reckoned as many. “Very many, World-Honored One” is the elder’s reply. This section only sets up a simile as an introduction to what follows. For using countless grains of sand to figure the great number of worlds is all done to bring out what follows: that the minds of living beings are many and the Tathāgata knows them all.
(Ji) Next, knowing them all.
[The Buddha said to Subhūti: "All the minds of the living beings in all those lands, in all their various kinds, the Tathāgata knows them all.

Wherever the sutra marks a phrase with “the Buddha said to,” it is a solemn phrase, causing the reader to take what follows solemnly. “All those” means “so many,” referring to the immeasurable spoken of above. Immeasurable lands is another way of saying immeasurable worlds, but world is the general name and land the particular name. Here, about to speak of living beings, the text says “lands” and not “worlds.” Why? Because using the particular name “land” shows that living beings have all kinds of differences: the lands of the ten directions and all the living beings in them with their various differences. It means that whatever the differences of race, kind, or bodily form among living beings, from the great gods and humans down to the small ants, their minds are all known.

The previous section did not merely say “worlds” but said “Buddha-worlds,” which likewise contains a profound intent. One should know that the world’s being held together and not destroyed is indeed due to living beings’ karma, but were it not for the power of the Buddha’s compassion and awe-inspiring spirit to gather and sustain it, then given the foulness of living beings’ karma it would long since have become an unbearable state beyond reckoning. All living beings receive the Buddha’s grace without knowing it, just as creatures that move, fly, or swim receive their formation entirely as a gift of sunlight without knowing it. The saying goes: thunder and rain, dew and lightning are all Heaven’s grace. Heaven’s grace in truth comes from the Buddha’s bestowal of grace. Consider what the great Mahāyāna sutras say: Brahmā kings, Indra, and even the sun and moon deities and all the gods all make vows before the Buddha to protect and sustain living beings. Thus we know that the world’s being held together truly depends on the power of the Buddha’s compassionate, awe-inspiring grace. In sum, every single character, every phrase, every term, every title in this sutra contains wondrous meaning and must not be overlooked. The worlds and lands are already as many as immeasurable; how much more the living beings within them, whose number can never be spoken of. How much more still the minds of living beings. Truly it is what is called unutterable and unutterable. Why? Since it is the mind of a living being, thought follows thought without pause; even of one living being, how many are his minds beyond counting, let alone the minds of unutterable living beings. Hence the text sums them up as “various kinds.” “Various kinds” means that their differences are so many that no number can be stated. The previous section went from one Ganges River to the countless sand within it, from that countless sand to countless Ganges Rivers, from those countless Ganges Rivers to the immeasurable sand within them, and again from that immeasurable sand to immeasurable worlds. This section again goes from immeasurable worlds to the unutterable living beings within them, and then from those unutterable living beings to their unutterable and unutterable minds. The reason for speaking in such successive layers is both to reveal the meaning of not one and to set up what follows about not different, and also to introduce the Tathāgata’s knowing them all. That one who knows even such unfathomably various things knows them all, how could this be a knowledge of differences? The World-Honored One knows them in terms of thusness. Hence it is said that the Tathāgata knows them all. This meaning corresponds to the Tathāgata’s speaking below, and altogether shows that a bodhisattva should know in this way. What does the Tathāgata’s knowing them all mean? The section below under “why” precisely makes its meaning clear; how the minds of living beings actually are is precisely made clear in the further section below under “what is the reason.”
(Chen) Next, the explanation that it is not mind.
["Why? The Tathāgata says that all minds are not mind; therefore they are called mind.

“All minds” refers to the various kinds of mind in the previous section. The phrase “are not mind” speaks in terms of nature and covertly points to their not being the true mind; the true mind is the nature. The phrase “are called” speaks in terms of marks and means that such minds are merely provisionally named mind, covertly pointing to their being the deluded mind. The deluded mind is the mind that flows onward, spoken of below. Flowing onward has marks, and so it is said to be “called.” A name is a mark and a name. Here one should not expose the true and the deluded too plainly but can only speak in a veiled way. Since this is the deluded and not the true, the section below will state the reason why; to expose it here would make the section below redundant.

“Why?” is the Buddha’s own question. The question: the minds of living beings are of various kinds, why does the Tathāgata know them all? “The Tathāgata says” is his own answer. The answer: although they are said to be of various kinds, the Tathāgata knows that in reality they can be summed up as one kind, namely that all are not mind but merely provisionally named mind. On the surface the sutra text seems only to explain that the Tathāgata can know them all, without stating why he knows them all. In fact the reason is already shadowed forth in it. What is the reason? It lies in the two words “Tathāgata.” For the Tathāgata is the meaning of the thusness of all dharmas. Thusness is true suchness; true suchness is the nature of one substance. Having realized the nature of one substance, one attains the great perfect mirror wisdom. Therefore when any living being gives rise to a thought, it is perfectly distinct in the Buddha’s mirror-mind. Moreover the Buddha’s mind is without thought, and so he knows that whatever gives rise to thought is not mind. This is the reason for knowing them all. The previous section says the Tathāgata knows them all; this section says the Tathāgata says: precisely making clear that he knows in accordance with the meaning of thusness and speaks in accordance with the meaning of thusness.

Long ago in the time of Emperor Daizong of the Tang, a monk came from the West whom the people called the Tripitaka of the Great Ear. He claimed to have the power of knowing others’ minds. Daizong asked National Master Zhong of Nanyang, a great worthy of the Chan school, to test him. After they had sat a short while, the master asked, “Where is this old monk now?” He answered, “You are at the Western River watching boat races.” After a while the master asked again. He answered, “You are on the Tianjin Bridge watching a monkey show.” The master fell silent for a while and asked again, and then he did not know. The master scolded him: “Where is your knowledge of others’ minds now?” The power of knowing others’ minds is knowing what is in another’s mind. National Master Zhong first deliberately gave rise to a thought, now at the Western River, now on the bridge, to test him. Then when he fell silent, he gave rise to no thought. Since no thought arose, there was no way to know. With this as proof, that the Tathāgata knows them all needs no further argument.

One should know that the thoughts of ordinary beings are known even by ghosts and spirits; as the saying goes, no sooner does a scheming mind stir than the spirits already know it. As for subtle thoughts, only bodhisattvas and arhats can know them; as for the Buddha, there is nothing he does not know. Those who do not understand the intent of National Master Zhong’s scolding think he disbelieved in the power of knowing others’ minds. That is not so. His intent in scolding came to no more than two things. One should know that spiritual powers must not be clung to; to cling to them means, at best, showing off and bringing harm, and at worst, being possessed by demons and going mad. This is spoken in terms of principle. National Master Zhong had very many disciples, and Daizong was also his disciple. To prize the strange and love the marvellous is the common feeling of people. If the great assembly made much of such things, it would be an obstacle to cultivation and might also harm the Dharma-gate. This is spoken in terms of fact. This Tripitaka of the Great Ear’s powers were surely not high. Had they been high, he could have known even a subtle thought once it arose, and even when no thought arose he could have known that no thought had arisen. How could it be that when National Master Zhong fell silent he was bewildered and did not know what to say? Since his powers were not high, and he claimed in the midst of the assembly to have attained them, his conduct came close to showing off and plainly violated the Buddha’s command. For the Buddha commanded his disciples not to display spiritual powers unless there were no other way. This was the master’s intent in rebuking him. One should know that the three insights and six spiritual powers are a matter of course for students of the Buddha, but in cultivation one should not make much of them for fear of entering the demonic path. When ignorance is exhausted, spiritual powers are attained of themselves, and after attaining them one should not lightly let others know, for fear of giving those who fabricate oddities a pretext, with many later troubles.

Above, from sand to river, to sand again, to worlds, to lands, to living beings, the facts and marks are various and not one, yet all are gathered up in the minds of living beings; this is not merely to show that outside the mind there are no dharmas. For the river is spoken of to figure the flowing of thoughts, and sand to figure their density. Sand made into rivers figures thoughts going from the subtle to the manifest; the sand of rivers figures thoughts going from the general to the particular. Going from river sands to worlds, lands, and living beings figures that the thoughts of living beings both flow onward without pause, like a river, and are stuck fast and unyielding, like earth; are both infinitely fine and trivial, like sand, and race without limit, like worlds; that some arise of themselves, like the sands of rivers, and some are set up and made, like lands; that there is source and stream, root and branch, the general, like worlds, the particular, like lands, and the particular within the particular, like living beings. Hence it speaks of minds of various kinds. As said above, there are two layers of neither one nor different. Outwardly, mountains, rivers, and the great earth; inwardly, the five aggregates and the bodily form: their facts and marks are utterly not one, yet as things manifested by the minds of living beings they are not different. Further, the thoughts of living beings are of many various kinds, which is not one, yet all are not mind, which again is not different. All this is what one who is awakening should understand. Yet these two layers of neither one nor different are still only an introduction to what follows. In sum, the phrases of neither one nor different, since they reveal that every dharma is thus, thereby reveal that there is no fixed dharma. They cause the practitioner, in regard to all dharmas, to look and use them flexibly without giving rise to rigid clinging. Hence the Buddha sometimes speaks of oneness to reveal not different, sometimes of difference to reveal not one, sometimes of both oneness and difference to reveal that though not one they are not different and though not different they are not one, and sometimes denies both oneness and difference to reveal that even neither one nor different cannot be spoken of. All this is nothing but to dispel emotional clinging. Dispelling and again dispelling, until the practice reaches the point where nothing can be spoken of, one realizes the thusness of all dharmas. His statements about existence and non-existence all carry this meaning. In sum, they make clear that one must not cling anywhere, in order to cure living beings’ sickness of clinging everywhere. Whether worldly or world-transcending dharmas, one should contemplate in this way and practice in accordance with this meaning.
(Chen) Third, the summary that it cannot be grasped.
["What is the reason? Subhūti, the past mind cannot be obtained, the present mind cannot be obtained, the future mind cannot be obtained."]

Cannot be grasped means cannot be obtained. Of the three phrases about past, present, and future mind, in the commentary of the Tang master Huijing the first phrase is the past, the second the future, and the third the present; the treatise of Bodhisattva Asaṅga is the same. Though the order differs, the general purport is unaffected.

This section explains the reason why it is not mind. Past, present, and future are called the three periods. A period is a boundary, a limit. The past is not the present or the future, the present is not the past or the future, and the future is not the present or the past; each has its boundary, and so they are called the three periods. Since thoughts have three periods, they are said to flow onward. Flowing onward means that the mind is like water, wave pushing wave forward, moving and flowing without cease. This is the formation aggregate among form, feeling, conception, formations, and consciousness. Formation means movement, flowing onward. Because thoughts do not pause for an instant, they are said to flow onward; because they flow onward, there are past, present, and future. Yet the past has already gone, the present does not abide, and the future has not yet come, and so none can be obtained. Strictly speaking, there is only past and future, and no present, for instant by instant it has already become past; how could there be anything to obtain? Cannot be obtained makes clear that it is empty right where it is. As for the true mind, it is permanently abiding and unmoving and is by no means flowing onward. But because living beings from beginningless time until now have never been apart from thought, and thought is a thing of arising and ceasing, it becomes flowing onward, and so it is not mind; it is said not to be the permanently abiding true mind. The mind of arising and ceasing is deluded and not true because the true mind is fundamentally neither arising nor ceasing. Since arising and ceasing do not pause, how could there be any real thing? Hence it is said to be called mind.

The previous section made perfect vision clear, causing those who do not understand the principle yet consider themselves right to understand that there is no right and wrong. That was still speaking of the naturalness of not clinging. Here, in making right knowledge clear, the reason why one must not cling is made clear. Hence it asks, “What is the reason?” The meaning of this section is this: when you grasp and cling to anything among all dharmas, in your own mind you surely think that you are the one who can grasp. You do not know that this very single thought of being able to grasp flows through the three periods and is empty right where it is. If the thought itself cannot be obtained, how much less can there be any grasping? Saying three times that it cannot be obtained is truly a heart-piercing phrase, directly leaving no place for the view of self to stand. The Śūraṅgama Sūtra says: “All living beings, from beginningless time, continue in birth and death because they do not know the permanently abiding true mind, the pure and luminous essence of the nature. They use all manner of deluded thoughts, and these thoughts are not true, and so there is revolution.” One should know that living beings from beginningless time take the deluded to be the true, and so bring about the revolution of birth and death, because all is made by mind alone, the pure and luminous essence of the nature. The misery of revolution truly comes about because their minds revolve through arising and ceasing. Once one mentions marks, there must be arising and ceasing. The important thing is that the mind does not move along with marks; movement is formation, what is called flowing onward. Then all suffering is removed. What is called understanding birth and death and escaping revolution is the mind understanding and the mind escaping.

Therefore the first step in cultivation is to understand this principle clearly and distinguish what is true from what is deluded. In fact it is very easy to distinguish. In shallow terms: to discriminate and cling is deluded, and not to discriminate and cling is true. In deeper terms: the true mind is without thought, and a thought arising is delusion, since it is through formation as a condition for consciousness that a thought arises as the root of discrimination and clinging. What is called cultivation and realization is nothing else than removing delusion. How is delusion removed? By transcending thought. When thought is transcended, discrimination and clinging disappear of themselves, the true mind appears of itself, and birth and death are ended of themselves. Transcend one part and see one part; when the transcending is ultimate, the seeing is ultimate too. The reason all living beings take the deluded to be the true is that they do not know it cannot be obtained. Why do they not know? Because their minds are coarse and they do not discern that it is arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing, continuing instant by instant. If they knew it continues instant by instant, they would know it is flowing onward and cannot be obtained. Since it cannot be obtained, what is the use of clinging to it? Moreover they think they can grasp, when in fact there is nothing to grasp; they merely increase their karmic force. Truly this is foolish and pitiable. This principle is known and spoken only by the Buddha, and it is what practitioners most urgently need to awaken to. Therefore in making right knowledge clear, this matter is spoken of first, because it is the key to becoming ordinary or becoming a sage. Seen in this way: although this sutra teaches transcending marks and transcending thoughts together, in reality it comes down to transcending thought, and it uses transcending marks only as the skillful means for transcending thought. Once thought is transcended, then seeing marks is seeing the nature; one may manifest marks according with conditions and broadly save living beings, with no obstruction at all. Why? Because once thoughts are transcended, in regard to marks, without transcending them one is already transcended.

The meaning of this section is unfathomably deep. The “cannot be obtained” spoken of above clarifies the meaning in terms of the deluded mind, but the Buddha’s greatest purpose in speaking this section does not lie there. What is the purpose? It is to enable students, by means of delusion, to realize the truth and suddenly accord with the unborn. Why is this said? The mind that flows through the three periods is what is called ignorance as the condition for formation. Ignorance is non-awakening. All living beings at first do not awaken to the fact that thought follows thought in flowing onward, and so they follow along in discrimination and clinging. Discrimination becomes the sixth consciousness, and clinging becomes the seventh consciousness; this is formation as the condition for consciousness. When the text here says the Tathāgata knows, it is telling students that they should know in this way. To know is to awaken. And it tells them: the mind that flows onward is empty right where it is and truly cannot be obtained. This is precisely to make students awaken quickly and turn directly to the place where nothing can be obtained, contemplating and entering there. Then, utterly clear and utterly still, this very moment is the permanently abiding true mind. As it is said, when the mad mind does not rest, rest is itself bodhi. Hence the meaning of this section is to make clear the most perfect and most sudden Dharma-gate that points directly upward.

Long ago the Second Patriarch asked the First Patriarch for the method of pacifying the mind. The patriarch said, “Bring me your mind and I will pacify it for you.” He said, “Seeking the mind, it cannot be obtained at all.” The patriarch said, “I have pacified your mind for you.” This has the same flavor of Dharma as what is said here. One should know it in this way and not betray the Buddha’s grace. Hence the previous section’s phrase that all are not mind and are called mind can also make the true mind clear at the same time. For the true mind has no name and no marks; it is only one emptiness and stillness. To call it the true mind is also not mind; it is merely a provisional name. That is why the ancient worthy said: describe it as a thing and you have already missed it.

Seen in this way, this section likewise possesses two layers of neither one nor different. Past mind, present mind, and future mind are not one; that all cannot be obtained is not different. Further, the flowing mind and the permanently abiding mind are not one; knowing that it cannot be obtained and is empty and still right where it is, is not different. Together with what the previous section said, this makes four layers in all. One should know that the Buddha’s speaking of these four layers in such detail is to reveal the skillful means of cultivating contemplation. What are the skillful means? First contemplate the not-oneness of the dharmas of the vessel-world and the faculties and body, such as the river sands, and dissolve them into the mind that living beings all possess in common and that is not different. Then advance to contemplate the not-oneness of thoughts in their various kinds, and dissolve them into the not-different “all are not and are merely named” of all those minds. Further contemplate that the reason all minds are not mind is that the not-oneness of the three periods flows onward, and dissolve it into the non-obtaining of the not-different three periods. One should know that not different is the meaning of thusness. Step by step, from not-one contemplating not-different, one step by step tends toward true suchness. Then further contemplate deeply that the flowing mind and the permanently abiding mind, though said to be not one, are only the difference of nature and marks; then transcending marks and meeting the nature, one dissolves into the great emptiness that is fundamentally unobtainable, and what difference could remain? Then, still and luminous, luminous and still, not a single thought arises. Not a single thought arising, the true mark is born. Is this not the cultivation that leaps straight in at one bound? Wondrous beyond words. Now I point it out one by one for you all.

If one can cultivate contemplation and practice in accordance with this meaning, one advances a thousand li a day, and there is no need to say more. One should know that the four layers of meaning go deeper with each layer, and that step by step entering not-different from not-one is step by step removing discrimination and clinging, and also step by step becoming without self. When not a single thought arises, where can the self of persons or the self of dharmas remain? Truly this is the wondrous Dharma of no-self. If a bodhisattva does not penetrate here, where else should he penetrate?

This great section is about opening the Buddha’s right knowledge, causing one to open the Buddha’s right enlightenment. Therefore, hearing such a teaching, one should open in this way. Opening in this way is awakening in this way; awakening in this way, one can realize in this way. What perfect and sudden great Dharma could surpass this? The next great section on all dharmas arising from conditions should likewise be opened and awakened in this way. One opens and awakens toward the mind’s activity, the other opens and awakens toward all dharmas. Advancing on both sides at once, mind and object both perish and self and dharmas are both empty. This is precisely what is meant by no mark of self, no mark of dharmas, and also no mark of no-dharmas; and one who transcends all marks is then named a Buddha. The doctrinal schools have many famous phrases, but none so direct and to the point; the Chan school’s blows and shouts fly back and forth, but none so manifest and clear. I wish to encourage you all in this together.

(Mao) Next, making clear that all dharmas arise from conditions. This has two parts: (Chen) first, clarifying no-nature in terms of the reward of merit; next, clarifying emptiness of substance in terms of the gift of Dharma.

The title of this great section contains a great deal of meaning. It should first be explained point by point, so that once we enter the text it is easier to grasp. The previous section on the mind’s activity clarifies the meaning in terms of the inner mind; this section on all dharmas clarifies the meaning in terms of outer objects. The facts and marks of outer objects are very many, and so they are called all dharmas. All dharmas are too many to count, so where should one begin? Now by clarifying the meaning in terms of the reward of merit and the gift of Dharma, one can encompass all dharmas. For once the meaning of the reward of merit is clear, the matters that are not the reward of merit can be inferred; giving encompasses the six perfections, and the six perfections encompass all practices; and among giving, the gift of Dharma is supreme. If the meaning of the gift of Dharma is clear, all the six perfections and all practices can be inferred. The gift of Dharma is a good practice, and once the meaning of good practice is clear, the matters that are not good practice can also be inferred.
As for the two words “arising from conditions,” they should be set out point by point. When I just said that the meaning is very great, I was referring to this.

(1) In the Buddhist scriptures the two words “cause and condition” are sometimes spoken of separately and sometimes together. Spoken of separately, cause is cause and condition is condition, and the two must not be confused; spoken of together, to speak of cause includes condition and to speak of condition includes cause. For the direct cause is called cause and the indirect cause is condition, and so they can be spoken of together. The single expression “arising from conditions” is spoken of together, what is called dharmas born of causes and conditions. Dharmas born of causes and conditions means that the arising of all dharmas is never apart from causes and conditions and never comes about without any reason. Hence dharmas are the fruits born of causes and conditions; dharmas born of causes and conditions is no different from saying that all dharmas do not go beyond cause and effect. Merit and the fulfilled bodily marks clarify the meaning in terms of the reward of fruit, while the gift of Dharma clarifies the meaning in terms of causal practice. Since all dharmas do not go beyond cause and effect, this encompasses all dharmas completely.

(2) All dharmas arise from conditions means that all dharmas are fundamentally unborn, and only because causes and conditions gather do a mark of arising falsely appear. This is meant to make clear that all dharmas are false marks and not the true nature, since the nature is inherently possessed and eternally constant and does not arise from the gathering of causes and conditions. Hence the title says “no nature,” meaning that they have only marks and no nature. One should know that the word “nature” in Buddhist books always refers to the nature of the mind-essence and is utterly unlike what worldly books call the nature or character of things. And since all dharmas are nothing but falsely manifesting marks, one may know that all dharmas in their very substance are like an illusion, like a transformation, like flowers in the sky, like the moon in water, and by no means real things. Hence the title says “emptiness of substance.” The word “substance” here refers to the thing itself, like what ordinary speech calls the thing in itself, and does not mean the essence of the nature. Therefore the meaning of arising from conditions reveals that they have marks and no nature and are empty in their very substance. Merit and the fulfilled bodily marks readily reveal the meaning of no-nature, while the gift of Dharma readily reveals the meaning of emptiness of substance; hence the assignment. From this one may know that to speak of arising from conditions is no different from speaking of cannot be obtained, and to speak of cannot be obtained is no different from speaking of arising from conditions. Why? Because the mind’s activity is also a dharma arising from conditions; this is what is called ignorance as the condition for formation. Now living beings cling everywhere, and the moment one speaks of clinging there is a grasper and a grasped. Spoken of from the side of the grasper, there is nothing but deluded thoughts; spoken of from the side of the grasped, they are all dharmas. Now the Buddha tells you: do you think there is one who grasps? The mind’s activity cannot be grasped; the very thought of grasping is empty right where it is. And he tells you again: do you think there is something grasped? All dharmas arise from conditions; the grasped dharmas too are empty in their very substance. Such a revelation is precisely uprooting living beings’ clinging views from the foundation. If one who is awakening understands this principle, the view of self can melt away like ice. Why? The view of self arises from clinging to the real; once one takes deluded thoughts as the true mind and also takes all dharmas as truly existent, the view of self cannot be dispelled. Therefore to dispel the clinging to self, the most wondrous practice is to contemplate emptiness. The Buddha is called the King of Physicians and also the King of Emptiness, meaning that he can cure living beings’ sickness of clinging to the real.

(3) Both arising from conditions and cannot be obtained make clear the meaning of being empty. This is as said above. Yet although the general purport is not different, the breadth and narrowness of their meaning is not one. For the meaning of cannot be obtained clarifies only being empty, while the meaning of arising from conditions clarifies being empty and also clarifies being provisional. Deluded thoughts are the cause of becoming ordinary; to end birth and death and realize the fruit of sagehood, one must cut off thought. Hence it is fitting only to speak of cannot be obtained and not to speak of arising from conditions. All dharmas should certainly not be grasped and clung to, nor should they be annihilated; hence it is fitting only to speak of arising from conditions and not to speak of cannot be obtained. What is meant by being at once empty and provisional? One should know that all dharmas are merely arising from conditions and are fundamentally empty; this is why the text says “is not.” Yet since they have already arisen from conditions, they are not without provisional existence; this is why the text says “is named.” Therefore dharmas and non-dharmas alike should not be grasped. Moreover, although all dharmas are empty in substance, since they arise from conditions they are an emptiness that is precisely provisional; therefore although they are by no means real, their facts and marks are solemnly present. This is why living beings find it hard to escape the deluded path. And although all dharmas precisely arise from conditions and yet are empty in substance, this is a provisionality that is precisely empty; therefore although the facts and marks are solemnly present, they are by no means real. This is why the practitioner should urgently awaken. How does one awaken? By not clinging to emptiness or existence. How can one not cling? The essential point is transcending marks and transcending thoughts. Only by transcending marks and transcending thoughts can one accord with conditions without changing and be unchanging while according with conditions.

(4) It was said above that the two sections on the mind’s activity and on all dharmas reveal the cultivation that leaps straight in at one bound. Yet there is also in them what, though not different, is not one, and this must be discerned. For entering directly at the place where the mind’s activity cannot be obtained is entering the empty and still essence of the nature; whereas entering directly at the place where all dharmas arise from conditions is entering the essence, marks, and function of emptiness according to reality and non-emptiness according to reality, which is to enter the virtue of the nature in which stillness and illumination are simultaneous. Yet only after attaining the essence can one give rise to function; non-emptiness must come forth from emptiness. If one does not transcend thought, one cannot even be still, let alone illuminate. Therefore in the gate of practice, students must not cling to emptiness or existence; and in the gate of contemplation, they must be empty all the way through. This principle must not go unknown. In sum, because the mind’s activity cannot be grasped, one should transcend thought; because all dharmas arise from conditions, one should transcend the marks of both extremes, emptiness and existence. Did I not say before that transcending thought is the ultimate of transcending marks, and transcending marks is the skillful means for transcending thought? Therefore in one’s practice one should take transcending thought as the main thing. If one transcends it, the marks of the two extremes, emptiness and existence, are perfectly transcended without any need to speak of transcending them. Even so, one who transcends thought should also understand the meaning that all dharmas arise from conditions and are at once empty and provisional, as an aid. One should know that the mind-nature is fundamentally emptiness and existence simultaneous; hence the dharmas manifested by mind alone are also all emptiness and existence simultaneous. To contemplate all dharmas as arising from conditions, at once empty and existent, is no different from contemplating the mind-nature as at once empty and existent. If one knows only transcending thought and does not cultivate this contemplation, one may fall into one-sided emptiness and fail to reach stillness as illumination and illumination as stillness. Therefore after speaking of the mind’s activity being unobtainable, the text also speaks of all dharmas arising from conditions. This principle still more must not go unknown. This is the Buddha’s right knowledge, and it should be opened in this way.

(5) It was said above that the nature and all dharmas are not different in being at once empty and existent. Yet there is also in them what is not one, and this must be discerned. For the true mind is not only truly empty but also truly existent. Truly empty because it is apart from names and cut off from marks; truly existent because it is constant and unchanging. Those dharmas that arise from conditions are not so: there is fundamentally no such thing, and only a false mark appears; they are truly empty and provisionally existent. (Strictly speaking, one cannot even call this truly empty; one can only call it falsely empty, since the emptiness of all dharmas is formed by provisional existence. Since they are not real things, neither emptiness nor existence can be predicated of them. Here I follow the ancient meaning provisionally and call it truly empty and provisionally existent.) Because they are fundamentally empty, provisional existence is spoken of; because they are provisionally existent, we know they are fundamentally empty. In order to make clear that their emptiness and existence come about as mutually dependent and mutually contrasted, the text says that emptiness and existence are simultaneous. This is unlike the true mind, whose emptiness apart from names and cut off from marks and whose existence that is constant and unchanging are both absolute. Their being simultaneous and both possessed is in no way brought about by mutual dependence and mutual contrast. Hence it is called true, and hence it can be the essence of all dharmas. Further, since the true mind is eternally constant, it is said to be fundamentally unborn. If all dharmas are also called fundamentally unborn, it is because, falsely manifesting a mark of arising, they are formed as fundamentally unborn; in reality there is fundamentally no such thing, and there is no question of unborn. Hence although the name “fundamentally unborn” is not different, the one being true and the other false is likewise not one.

Someone may say: outside the mind there are no dharmas, and when the mind arises, all kinds of dharmas arise. This mind refers to the deluded mind. But then the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, having no deluded thoughts, can still manifest all kinds of objects and marks; how does this come about? Answer: the Buddhas and bodhisattvas truly have no thoughts, and all kinds of objects and marks are truly manifested by mind. This comes about because in the causal stage they made great compassionate vows to accord with conditions and save living beings. Hence after realizing the fruit, though they do not give rise to thought, by the power of the perfuming of their former compassionate vows they can respond to the faculties and accord with conditions, manifesting all kinds of objects and marks. This meaning is scattered throughout the sutras and treatises and in the Mahāyāna Calming and Contemplation. Therefore when cultivating the cause, one must fulfill compassionate vows and deeply contemplate the meaning of all dharmas arising from conditions, so that the perfuming becomes a seed, and only then can one manifest according with conditions within the great samādhi. The meanings spoken of above are all things the practitioner should understand. Otherwise one will surely doubt why thought is still not purified after realizing the fruit, or doubt that without thought there would be nothing manifested, or doubt why the true mind, being at once empty and existent and fundamentally unborn in the same way as all dharmas, should be the essence of all dharmas. Here I take the occasion to say a word about it.

(6) All the meanings spoken of since the opening of the sutra come to a thorough understanding of their why and wherefore through these two sections on the mind’s activity being unobtainable and on all dharmas arising from conditions. For the phrases about the three emptinesses and about all being is-not are because the mind’s activity cannot be obtained; and the phrases about not clinging to the two extremes and about all being is are because all dharmas arise from conditions. Hence this great section on opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is in truth the most important part of the whole sutra. Everything said before and after is nothing but opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. The faithful have faith in this, the understanding understand this, the cultivating cultivate this, and the realizing realize this. Only by joining faith, understanding, practice, and realization together is the work of the word “opening” accomplished. Faith is the first opening, and understanding, then practice, then realization are the ultimate opening.

blocks.text: The Dharmadhātu Pervades and Transforms All, Part Nineteen

inline.s: (Chen) First, clarifying no-nature in terms of the reward of merit. This has two parts: (Ji) first, clarifying merit; next, clarifying the reward body. (Ji) The first again has two: (Wu) first, clarifying the causes and conditions of merit; next, clarifying that it arises when conditions gather.
(Wu) First, clarifying the causes and conditions of merit.

["Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill three thousand great chiliocosms with the seven treasures and give them away, would that person, by this cause and condition, attain much merit?" "So it is, World-Honored One. That person, by this cause and condition, would attain very much merit."]

Giving away the treasures of worlds has been spoken of before. Developing the meaning of arising from conditions from what has already been said contains a subtle intent. For it shows that all the marks of dharmas spoken of above should be pervaded by the meaning of arising from conditions. The Madhyamaka Treatise says: dharmas born of causes and conditions are at once empty and provisional. One should know that not only are the dharmas produced at once empty and provisional; the causes and conditions too are at once empty and provisional. Because causes and conditions are at once empty and provisional, though one does not cling to marks one should practice giving; this is why it was said before that one should practice giving without dwelling anywhere. Because causes and conditions are at once provisional and empty, though one practices giving one should not cling to marks; this is why it was said before that one should give without dwelling in marks. Because the dharmas produced are at once empty and provisional, though they are empty in their very substance they arise when conditions gather; this is why the text has repeatedly said “is named.” Because the dharmas produced are at once provisional and empty, though they arise when conditions gather they are empty in their very substance; this is why the text has repeatedly said “is not.”

This section clarifies the meaning of arising from conditions in general. What is meant by “in general”? It speaks from the causes and conditions of giving through to merit, and merit is the dharma produced by the causes and conditions of giving. Hence giving is the cause and merit the fruit; cause and fruit are spoken of together, and so it is called general. Then the reward body below, which speaks only in terms of fruit, allows one to infer that a fruit must have a cause. The section on the gift of Dharma seems only to speak of cause, yet one can also infer that cause and effect are inexhaustible. For only when the giver, the recipient, and the hearer of the Dharma-gift each have their causes and conditions and all gather together does this matter of the Dharma-gift occur. Thus this one Dharma-gift is produced by the gathering of countless causes and conditions, and the fruits each will obtain in the future are again produced by the causes and conditions of this one Dharma-gift. Is this not cause and effect inexhaustible?

Giving and the rest are great matters of the Buddhist gate, yet they are still not apart from arising from conditions and not apart from cause and effect; how much more so all other dharmas. Hence the text speaks in terms of these few matters to set out an example. What is called “general” has yet another meaning. The present section speaks loosely of merit, while the next section speaks of the reward body. To realize the reward body may indeed be called much merit. The present section speaks loosely of giving, while the next section again speaks specifically of the gift of Dharma. Both are nothing other than making the present section concrete. Hence one may also judge the present section to be general and the two sections on the reward body and the gift of Dharma to be particular.

In the first half of the sutra, the elder’s replies mostly say “no.” Even where he does not answer “no,” he never once answers “so it is.” In the second half, only in opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision does he answer “so it is” most often. (Apart from that, there is only the one place where he answers “so it is” to the question of contemplating the Tathāgata by the thirty-two marks.) Every character of this sutra contains profound meaning, and one may know that wherever he answers “so it is” it is by no means a casual remark. It in fact takes up what has been said before and expresses the meaning that all dharmas are thus and all is so. It was said before that “all is thus and so” makes clear the melting of marks and the meeting of the nature; the meaning made clear by this arising from conditions of all dharmas likewise intends the melting of marks and the meeting of the nature. The elder deeply understood the meaning and purport, and so first answered “so it is.” He then said that this person, by this cause and condition, attains very much merit. This precisely directs the practitioner to grasp the principle of all dharmas arising from conditions, so as to penetrate the fact that all dharmas are one thusness. For the principle of arising from conditions is precisely being at once empty and provisional. To contemplate being at once empty and provisional, so as to accord with emptiness according to reality and non-emptiness according to reality, is to melt the marks of all dharmas and meet the nature of one thusness.

It was said before: giving without dwelling in marks brings merit beyond reckoning. Now it says: he attains very much merit. Very much means beyond reckoning. The sutra’s purport leans toward the next section; what this section says is only to prepare the ground for the next section. Hence the layer of not dwelling in marks is not mentioned here but is mentioned in the next section.
(Wu) Next, clarifying that it arises when conditions gather.
["Subhūti, if merit were real, the Tathāgata would not say that much merit is attained. Because merit is not real, the Tathāgata says that much merit is attained.

This section is the Buddha’s true intent; the previous section was spoken precisely to introduce this one. The wording and purport of this section are deep and fine, and it must be clarified in several layers.

The previous section already made clear that merit is a dharma arising from conditions. Since it arises only when conditions gather, how could it be real? If it were real, it would not be arising from conditions. And if it were not arising from conditions, there would be no path by which merit could be attained, since no dharma ever comes about without a reason. Hence it says: if merit were real, the Tathāgata would not say that much merit is attained.

“Because” means “on account of.” “Not” means “not real,” directly answering the “real” above. It means that because merit is a dharma arising from conditions, at once empty and provisional and not real, any living being who can only practice the six perfections of giving and deeply plant causes and conditions will, when causes and conditions gather, have merit arise. Gathering means maturing. Hence it says: because merit is not real, the Tathāgata says that much merit is attained.

The two occurrences of the word “says” in the sutra deserve attention; they show that on the surface it speaks of merit while at the core it speaks of giving. Why? If one clings to merit as real, one does not know it is a dharma arising from conditions; not knowing it arises from conditions, one does not know to lay stress on the cause. If one does not cultivate the cause of giving, where will the fruit of merit come from? Hence the Tathāgata does not say that much merit is attained. But one fails to realize that precisely because merit is empty in its very substance and not real, it is a dharma arising from conditions that is at once empty and provisional. Therefore one who wishes to obtain the fruit need only cultivate the cause; if one diligently practices giving, merit will come of itself. Hence the Tathāgata says that much merit is attained.

With what has been said above, the great purport of the sutra is already clear, yet it has still not been spoken through. Why? Because only the relation of attaining and not attaining has been spoken of, while the relation of much and little has not yet been touched. One should know that the Buddha’s teaching of arising from conditions stresses causing people to penetrate thoroughly that all dharmas are at once empty and provisional, so as to penetrate no-self and melt marks into the meeting of the nature. This layer of principle must first have its origin and development made clear, and then it is easy to understand.

Every dharma is without exception born of causes and conditions, so merit arises from conditions and giving also arises from conditions. But if the cause and condition of merit is giving, what is the cause and condition of giving? One should know that the cause and condition of giving is the resolving of the mind. When the resolve is small, the giving is small and the merit is small; when the resolve is great, the giving is great and the merit is great. But how is the resolve great? By not dwelling in marks. When the mind dwells somewhere, it is bound; when it does not dwell, it is unbound and without limit, and so it is great. Therefore to give without dwelling in marks, one must first not dwell in marks regarding merit. If one fixes one’s attention on merit, one takes merit to be real (real means truly existent) and so dwells in marks. To practice giving while dwelling in marks regarding merit is to give for the sake of merit, and then the giving too dwells in marks. The World-Honored One’s speaking of this section is to develop the earlier teaching of giving without dwelling in marks even more thoroughly, and it is nothing less than exposing the root of the sickness in those who give while dwelling in marks. For the reason giving dwells in marks is nothing but greed for merit.

The three words “the Tathāgata says” in the text are very important; they mean that he speaks in accordance with the meaning of thusness. For if one has not penetrated the principle of arising from conditions, and knows only that by the cause and condition of giving one can attain merit, and so greedily seeks merit in order to practice giving, then one is greatly mistaken. One fails to realize that the Buddha’s teaching of arising from conditions is to make one realize that dharmas arising from conditions are at once empty and provisional, so that one does not cling to any dharma and dissolves into the nature of one thusness. If one takes merit to be real, one will inevitably greedily seek merit in order to practice giving and so dwell in marks. Dwelling in marks, one seeks outwardly and goes against the nature. Then by the cause and condition of giving there will indeed be merit, but by the cause and condition of dwelling in marks what one obtains is nothing but worldly merit within the three realms; even if one is born in the highest heaven, it is in the end a cause of suffering. Hence, in accordance with the meaning of thusness, he does not say that much merit is attained.

If one thoroughly understands the principle of arising from conditions, contemplating all dharmas as at once empty and provisional and at once provisional and empty, then there is not even a thought of merit.
