(In the text, one side is clearly the reverse and one the obverse, spoken in opposition; since the reverse side speaks of “real,” the obverse should also have a “not real,” and so I explain “not” as “not real.” Yet the sutra text after all only says “not,” and so one should supply the further meaning of “no thought.” The meaning of no thought is more thorough and should be spoken of here.) One practices the three kinds of giving that transcend marks solely for the benefit of living beings. Then one cultivates both merit and wisdom, and is complete in compassion and insight, and must attain merit and virtue that are inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless: the fruit of supreme enlightenment. In accordance with the meaning of thusness, one’s attainment of merit is great indeed.

Contemplating the purport of this sutra, it is fully evident that the principle of cause and effect must be thoroughly understood. If one knows only the shallow and crude teaching of cause and effect without penetrating its principle, then a small cause yields a small fruit. One should know that the cause and effect taught by the Buddha can by no means be regarded as on a par with the cause and effect spoken of in non-Buddhist scriptures or worldly books. The principle of cause and effect spoken of in the Buddhist sutras is thorough and perfect and extremely subtle; it is always explained by the principle of the three truths, being at once empty, provisional, and the Middle, or by the principle of the two truths such as the eight negations. Only when the principles of the two truths and the three truths are clear can the Buddha’s cause and effect be thoroughly understood. Only then does one know that the principle of cause and effect taught by the Buddha is vast, perfect, and wondrous, and that nothing worldly or world-transcending falls outside it. Only then does one know that cause and effect are to be feared: a single thought arising and one already falls into cause and effect, so why wait for it to be carried into action? Only then does one know that the Buddhadharma is necessary for everyone; not only should students of the Buddha understand the Buddhist principle, but even one who wishes to become a person of character cannot fail to understand it, and one who wishes truly to understand worldly dharmas cannot but first understand the Buddhist principle. Only then does one know that transcending marks and transcending thoughts is of great importance, and one will certainly not ignore it or fear its difficulty, but can give rise to the great resolve, cultivate the supreme practice, and realize the wondrous fruit.

Today there are people of good will who mostly know to promote and clarify the teaching of cause and effect, collecting facts and printing and distributing books, hoping to save minds that are sinking and to turn back a dangerous course in the world. This is the best of undertakings and an extremely important one. Yet there are often those who will not set eyes on it, thinking it too shallow. Then why not seek it within the Mahāyāna Buddhadharma? Principles such as the two truths and the three truths are all the true exposition of the Buddha’s cause and effect and are the ultimate meaning of cause and effect. Understand a little and there is a little benefit; understand much and there is much benefit. In sum, the Buddha’s cause and effect can make a person a worldly good man, a worthy, a sage, and even a bodhisattva or a Buddha. How vast and perfect and wondrous it is.

blocks.text: Transcending Body and Marks, Part Twenty

inline.s: (Ji) Next, clarifying the reward body. This has two parts: (Wu) first, clarifying that the physical body is not the nature; next, clarifying that the marks and excellences are not the nature.
(Wu) First, clarifying that the physical body is not the nature.

["Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Buddha be seen by his fulfilled physical body?" "No, World-Honored One. The Tathāgata should not be seen by his physical body. Why? The Tathāgata says that the fulfilled physical body is not the fulfilled physical body; therefore it is called the fulfilled physical body."]
The popular editions read “should not be seen by the fulfilled physical body,” but the Tang dynasty manuscript of the sutra does not have the word “fulfilled,” and it may be omitted.

About the fulfilled physical body and the fulfilled marks in the next section, the ancients had various explanations. Some combined physical body and marks together and spoke of the sixteen-foot golden body, explaining it as the manifested body. Some took the physical body to refer to the eighty excellences and the marks to the thirty-two marks, which is also to understand it as the manifested body. Some said the physical body is the reward body and the marks are the manifested and transformation bodies. Only Master Datian in the early Qing said that the physical body and the marks should be explained in terms of the reward body. This explanation is the most refined and should be followed. For since the sutra says “fulfilled” of both the physical body and the marks, and “fulfilled” means perfect and complete, it refers unmistakably to the reward body of perfect practice and the adornment of ten thousand virtues. For the manifested and transformation bodies, such as the sixteen-foot golden body and the thirty-two marks, do not accord with the meaning of fulfilled practice and fulfilled adornment.

The separate speaking of body and marks contains an essential meaning. The physical body is called fulfilled precisely because its marks are fulfilled. Hence the physical body is what is adorned and the marks are what adorns. Speaking of them separately is meant to show that there is an adorner and an adorned, which is precisely a dharma arising from conditions. As for the inherently possessed nature, it is only one emptiness and stillness; since it is not a physical mark, how could there be any distinction between what adorns and what is adorned?

“No” is a living phrase, meaning that it may and also may not be. For the dharma body and the reward body are neither one nor different. If one converges on the nature that is not different, then it can be seen; if one clings to the marks that are not one, then it cannot be seen. Hence the text continues: the Tathāgata should not be seen by his physical body. Above it says “no” and below it says “should not,” and the two precisely echo each other, showing that there is no such thing as may or may not, only should not. The words “Tathāgata” and “by” both contain essential meaning. In saying “by,” the intent to cling to marks is plain. The Tathāgata is the meaning of the thusness of all dharmas, the nature that is not different; the physical body is a mark that is not one. How could one cling to a mark that is not one in order to see the nature that is not different? The words imply that if one dissolves the marks, then the nature can be seen.

The passage under “why” makes clear the meaning of “should not.” “The Tathāgata says” speaks in terms of the nature. Speaking in terms of the nature, he says the fulfilled physical body; then the physical body is merely the reward ripened from causes cultivated over many kalpas, a dharma arising from conditions. Arising from conditions is not the nature; it is at once provisional and empty. Hence it says “is not the fulfilled physical body.” Yet since it is the mark that the inherently possessed nature manifests by according with conditions in the ripening of cultivated causes, though it is empty in its very substance, being at once empty and provisional, its name and marks are solemnly present. Hence it says “is called the fulfilled physical body.” The next section’s “is not” and “is named” of the fulfilled marks should be explained in the same way. Altogether they make clear that the reward body is a dharma arising from conditions, at once provisional and empty, at once empty and provisional. If one does not understand the meaning of being at once provisional and empty, one will inevitably cling to marks and be blind to the nature, and then nature and marks will be separated and not one; how could one see the nature? If one does not understand the meaning of being at once empty and provisional, one will in turn cling to the nature and discard marks, and nature and marks will likewise be separated and not one; then what one sees is in fact not the whole nature that is neither with marks nor without marks. How could it be called seeing the nature? Therefore one must deeply understand the principle of arising from conditions, realize that the fulfilled physical body and the rest are at once provisional and empty and at once empty and provisional, and cling to neither extreme; then nature and marks are perfectly interfused and not different, and seeing marks is seeing the nature. What one sees is then the whole nature that is neither with marks nor without marks, that is, emptiness according to reality and non-emptiness according to reality.

The Tathāgata’s supreme reward body is still arising from conditions; one may know that no dharma is not arising from conditions, and therefore no dharma may be clung to, for clinging must fall into one extreme. Clinging is what is called grasping. The mind grasps because it gives rise to thought. Hence to be utterly without grasping, there is nothing but transcending thought. One should know that the purpose of the Buddha’s teaching that all dharmas arise from conditions is to make people realize the principle of being at once provisional and empty and at once empty and provisional, to know that no dharma can fundamentally be clung to nor need be clung to, and so to transcend thought. The reason for transcending thought is that cultivating the cause of transcending thought must yield the fruit of no-thought; this too is nothing but a dharma arising from conditions. No-thought is what is called Buddha-wisdom, true suchness. From this it is fully evident that worldly and world-transcending dharmas are all arising from conditions, that is, all cause and effect. Those without wisdom use evil causes to invite evil fruits, good causes to invite good fruits, small causes to invite small fruits, and outflows-causes to invite outflows-fruits. If one opens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, one can use supreme causes to invite supreme fruits. What is supreme? No-thought is. In sum, every dharma arises from conditions, and therefore every dharma is at once empty and provisional. Hence in regard to worldly and world-transcending dharmas alike one should cling to neither extreme. And to be thorough in not clinging, there is nothing but transcending thought. Further, worldly and world-transcending dharmas are all arising from conditions, and so the worldly and the world-transcending are not beyond cause and effect. Hence, taking transcending thought as the cause, one realizes the fruit of no-thought true suchness.

Wherever the text before and after says “is not” and “is named,” it is all to make this meaning clear, and all should be pervaded by what has been said above. Earlier, the meaning of all dharmas arising from conditions had not yet been plainly stated, and so it could not be developed so freely; now it should be penetrated in this way. One should know that the style of this sutra moves from the scattered to the whole, first deducing and then gathering up. Hence what was said before is confirmed by what is said after, and its meaning becomes clearer. This is what enables bodhisattvas to penetrate: it means that the later meaning should be used to penetrate the earlier meaning. In expounding the entire sutra, one must follow the order of shallow and deep and speak as the text proceeds. Hence when expounding the first half, one can only contain and include the great purport of the second half; one absolutely cannot forcefully expound the later meaning in the earlier exposition. Why? The earlier text has its own intent. If one only attends to the great purport and not to its threads, then the sutra’s meaning, which was originally well ordered, is spoken of in a confused and disorderly way, and instead leaves the hearers utterly bewildered. But when one reaches the later meaning, if one does not string together and gather up what was said before, it becomes loose sand; not only does the earlier exposition have no home, but the later exposition also shows no brilliance, and the hearers are again utterly bewildered.

If commentators fall into this fault, then reading them leaves one dazed and lost with no thread to follow. When the thread is not clear, to seek a deep understanding is hard indeed. In sum, the difficulty of expounding this sutra is the same before and after, yet the reasons for the difficulty before and after are not one. The difficulty of the earlier part is that the essential meanings mostly lie in the later text, and when expounding one often finds one’s hands tied, able only to take the shadow by lamplight behind the curtain and not to speak one’s fill. The difficulty of the later part is that the principle is deep and the states are fine, hard to describe in words, and one must everywhere attend to the layer of transcending names and cut off from marks; though one may speak one’s fill, one must not speak a single word to death and block people’s gate of awakening. In this assembly there are good teachers who have given rise to the great resolve to spread this sutra, and this principle must not go unknown to them.
(Wu) Next, clarifying that the marks and excellences are not the nature.

["Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by his fulfilled marks?" "No, World-Honored One. The Tathāgata should not be seen by his fulfilled marks. Why? The Tathāgata says that the marks are fulfilled and yet not fulfilled; therefore they are called the fulfilled marks."]

Excellence is another name for mark; it means that following a given physical mark one further distinguishes the various excellences of that mark, and so it is called the excellence that follows the form. Now saying “the fulfilled marks” already includes the excellences; if there were no excellences, they could not be called fulfilled marks. What is ordinarily spoken of as the thirty-two marks and the eighty excellences are the marks and excellences of the manifested body, whereas the marks and excellences of the reward body are as spoken of in the Chapter on the Ocean of Marks in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra. On the Tathāgata’s crown there are thirty-two jewel-adorned marks; on the brow, eyes, nose, teeth, lips, and neck there is one adorned mark each; the tongue has four marks; the mouth has five; the right shoulder two; the left shoulder three; the chest one, namely the auspicious svastika mark; the left and right of the chest together have ten; the left and right hands together have thirteen; the concealed organ one; the two hips, the two thighs, and the two shins together have six; the body hair one; the two feet together have thirteen. These come to ninety-seven wondrous marks in all, called the marks of a great man. To know their names and forms, one may consult the sutra text. Yet this is still a brief account; spoken in full, there are as many marks of a great man as there are motes of dust in ten oceans of flower-treasury worlds. For the marks and excellences of the reward body are immeasurable and boundless. What is here called fulfilled refers to this. The Avataṃsaka says: “Each and every part of the body is adorned with the wondrous marks of many treasures.” From the meaning of this sutra one may know that the name “fulfilled physical body” is precisely so called because the marks are fulfilled. Hence it was said before that the marks are what adorns and the physical body is what is adorned. The rest of the meaning is as before. All the meanings of “is not” and “is named” spoken of in the previous section pervade this one, and there is no need to repeat them. The marks being fulfilled is the fulfilled marks. That the Buddha’s physical body and marks are called supreme and foremost lies precisely in the two words “fulfilled,” and so the text inverts the order to bring out the meaning.

From the opening of the sutra to this point, there have been three passages of question and answer about bodily marks, and the meaning made clear each time is different. Let me now divide them into three layers and speak of them together so as to make them easy to penetrate, each layer deeper than the last.

(1) The first time he asked, “Can the Tathāgata be seen by bodily marks?” He said only the two words “bodily marks,” which includes all bodily marks and does not refer specifically to the Buddha’s bodily marks; and “Tathāgata” also refers generally to the self-nature and not specifically to the Buddha. The second time he asked, “Can the Tathāgata be seen by the thirty-two marks?” which refers specifically to the Buddha, but this speaks of the manifested body. This time the wording of the question is the fulfilled physical body and the fulfilled marks, which speaks of the Buddha’s reward body.

(2) The first question and answer directly follows the teaching that one should not dwell in marks, and so it says only that bodily marks are not bodily marks and does not say “is named,” in order to reveal that marks are all false and unreal and that therefore one should not dwell in them. The second question and answer, because it is precisely making clear that provisional names are not destroyed, says both “is not” and “is named,” revealing that in terms of nature it is not, while in terms of marks it is, and that one should not dwell in either extreme. This time, because it is precisely making clear that all dharmas arise from conditions, it likewise raises both “is not” and “is named,” revealing the meaning of dharmas arising from conditions in which emptiness and existence are simultaneous.

(3) The wording of the first two questions was: “Can the Tathāgata be seen by bodily marks?” and “Can the Tathāgata be seen by the thirty-two marks?” Tathāgata is a name for the virtue of the nature, and to see the Tathāgata is another way of saying to see the nature. One should know that the reason marks should not be dwelt in is in order to see the nature. The nature is real and marks are false; to pursue the false is to go against the true. Hence one who wishes to see the nature should not dwell in marks. Yet the first time, in clarifying that one should not dwell in marks in terms of bodily marks, this was because bodily marks are the most intimately connected with the nature: if even bodily marks are false, how much more the other marks; if one should not dwell even in bodily marks, how much less in the other marks. What is called not dwelling means that one should see the non-mark right in the mark, and that is not dwelling; and then one can see the nature. It does not mean destroying the marks and only then seeing. This holds for bodily marks, and it holds for all marks. This is the meaning made clear by the first question and answer.

The second time, that provisional names are not destroyed is said after transcending the mark of names and the mark of words. Hence it uses the names and words of the thirty-two marks to make clear the true meaning of transcending marks. It means that the nature of true suchness is a state beyond thought; it cannot be named by names, spoken by words, or marked by marks. Hence one should transcend names, words, and marks and realize it for oneself. Yet what is called transcending names, words, and marks means that one should know the nature is not reached by names and words; it does not mean that there are no names, no words, and no marks. One has only not to grasp at the false marks of names and words in one’s mind, and that is transcending; and then one sees the nature. Does not the Tathāgata’s manifested and transformation body plainly have the names and words of the thirty-two marks? And these marks are in fact manifested by the Tathāgata. Hence, by not clinging to the marks, one sees the Tathāgata. If one knows how to transcend the names and words of the manifested and transformation body’s thirty-two marks, one knows how to transcend the names and words of the marks of all dharmas. This is the meaning made clear by the second question and answer.

This time the first question asks whether the Buddha can be seen by the fulfilled physical body, and the second asks whether the Tathāgata can be seen by the fulfilled marks. In one place it says “Buddha” and in the other “Tathāgata,” both with essential meaning; and the first question should only say “Buddha” and the second only “Tathāgata,” and the two cannot be interchanged. Why? One should know that Buddha is a name for the virtue of the fruit. The fulfilled physical body is the body of the fruition reward, and so in speaking of the fulfilled physical body one should use the name Buddha, showing that this body is precisely the body rewarded to one who has realized the fruit and become a Buddha. Tathāgata is a name for the virtue of the nature. The fulfilled marks are the marks perfectly and luminously manifested by the virtue of the nature, and so in speaking of the fulfilled marks one should use the name Tathāgata, showing that these marks are precisely the marks manifested by one who has realized the nature of true suchness. Hence the first joins Buddha with the fulfilled physical body to make clear that cause and effect are not false, and the second joins Tathāgata with the fulfilled marks to make clear that nature and marks are one thusness.

I have repeatedly said that Master Kumārajīva’s translation of this sutra does not let a single character be set down carelessly, that every character contains essential meaning, and that no character may be overlooked. Looking at these several sections, this is all the more proven. But then, if this body is the reward body of the Buddha’s fruit, why should it not be seen by this body? One should know that the Buddha can be seen by a physical body, but how can the Buddha-nature be seen by a physical body? To see the Buddha one should see the Buddha-nature; how could it be merely seeing the Buddha’s body? Hence the text does not say that the Buddha should not be seen by a physical body but says that the Tathāgata should not be seen by a physical body, and this is why. The question whether the Buddha can be seen by a physical body is precisely to test and examine one’s standpoint: does one know how to see the Buddha of the dharma body, or does one know only how to see the Buddha of the physical body?

Since the fulfilled marks are the perfect manifestation of the virtue of the nature, why should one not see by the marks? One should know that although nature and marks are one thusness, when one speaks of marks they are not the nature. What is called perfect interfusion contains ordered arrangement, and one must not be vague and muddled. Hence if one dissolves the marks and contemplates the nature, then since there is no conception of marks, why should the nature not be seen? But if one clings to marks in order to see the nature, then there is only the conception of marks, and how can the nature be seen? Hence the text does not say that the Tathāgata cannot be seen by the fulfilled marks but says that the Tathāgata should not be seen by the fulfilled marks, and this is why. And the question whether the Tathāgata can be seen by the fulfilled marks is likewise to test and examine one’s standpoint: although nature and marks are not one, they are in truth not different; and although not different, they are in truth not one. Can one deeply know the meaning and purport of nature and marks and greatly open one’s perfect vision, clinging neither to oneness nor to difference?

Further, the wording of these two questions this time is greatly different from the wording of the two previous times, and so the meaning made clear is greatly different. The wording of the two previous questions asked whether the Tathāgata can be seen by bodily marks or by the thirty-two marks, all spoken from the side of the seer, that is, from the side of the causal stage. The two questions here ask whether the Buddha or the Tathāgata can be seen by the fulfilled physical body or the fulfilled marks, spoken from the side of the Buddha or Tathāgata, that is, from the side of the fruition stage. Hence the meaning should be clarified in terms of the fruition stage. How is it clarified? One should know that the Buddha’s realization of the fruit also comes about through dependent origination, let alone the physical body. The Tathāgata’s light of the nature illumines while ever still; how could there be marks? Hence both are said to be “is not.” And one should further know that since the cause is perfect and the fruit complete, there is the fulfilled physical body; and though it is still while illumining and illumines while still, there are still the fulfilled marks. Hence both are said to be “is named.” “Is not” reveals that it is an emptiness that is precisely provisional; “is named” reveals that it is a provisionality that is precisely empty. Not only does one not dwell in the two extremes; the two extremes are altogether interfused. This is what is called perfect middle. A bodhisattva who penetrates the dharma of no-self should know it in this way.

Nor is this all. One should know that the perfection of the marks is the manifestation of the perfect luminosity of the virtue of the nature; how could one cling to the idea that apart from the marks there is a separate dharma body? Hence it says “is named.” Yet how could one also cling to the idea that the marks arising from conditions are the dharma body? Hence it says “is not.” But then one should not even cling to the marks manifested by the Tathāgata in order to see the Tathāgata; then it is clear that one who clings to the marks of all dharmas arising from conditions cannot see the Tathāgata, and one may know that none of them should be clung to. One should know that the fulfilled physical body is the supreme reward of the ultimate fruit of enlightenment; how could one cling to the idea that apart from the physical body there is a separate Buddha-nature? Hence it says “is named.” Yet how could one also cling to the idea that the physical body arising from conditions is the Buddha-nature? Hence it says “is not.” But then one should not even cling to the adorned reward body in order to see the pure dharma body; then it is again clear that one who clings to the five aggregates of the suffering body arising from conditions cannot see the self-nature dharma body, and one may know all the more that one should not cling to it.

In sum, saying “is named” causes one not to cling to difference, and saying “is not” causes one not to cling to oneness. Not clinging to oneness or difference is perfect vision. When vision is perfect, knowledge is also right; when knowledge is right, vision is also perfect. If one knows that no dharma is not arising from conditions, then one sees that all dharmas are neither one nor different. Seeing that they are not different while not preventing their not being one, one sees that they are fundamentally one thusness yet arise as all dharmas; seeing that they are not one while not obstructing their not being different, one sees that although they are all dharmas they are all one thusness. One should penetrate it in this way.

It was said above that merit includes all good fruits, great or small; this reward body is the greatest and supreme among merits. Yet whether great or small, superior or inferior, all are clarified in terms of fruit. Clarifying in terms of fruit makes clear that none of them is not arising from conditions. Let me now sum up the essential meaning of the Buddha’s teaching of arising from conditions in three points, going deeper with each layer. (1) It causes one to know that worldly and world-transcending dharmas are all empty, and only cause and effect are not empty. Why? Because they all arise from conditions. Hence cause and effect are to be feared, and hence one should cultivate a supreme cause and realize a supreme fruit. (To realize means to set a term and attain it.) (2) Since all is empty and yet cause and effect are not empty, all dharmas are at once empty and provisional. Because they are provisional, a cause must have its fruit, and a supreme cause must yield a supreme fruit. Because they are empty, although cause and effect are supreme, one goes about it as if doing nothing at all. This is called deeply understanding cause and effect. (3) The Buddha’s teaching that all dharmas arise from conditions is meant to make clear that they are fundamentally unborn. If throughout the twelve periods of the day one does worldly dharmas while according with conditions and takes up world-transcending dharmas while according with conditions, yet keeps one eye fixed on the place where all dharmas are fundamentally unborn, looking there, and does not even think of oneself as the one who looks, but simply, at the very time of according with conditions in worldly and world-transcending dharmas, looks in this way, and at the very time of looking, accords with conditions in this way, then one may be allowed to be called a clever fellow. Inwardly, the mind of the three periods is gathered into cannot be obtained; outwardly, all dharmas are gathered into fundamentally unborn. Where can self and dharmas hide? Truly, one thing understood and a hundred things are done, and all under heaven is at peace. Our original teacher has taught us these Dharma-gates that cut straight across. We must shoulder them in one load and run with all our strength toward the goal. Do you not know the saying: the day has passed and life decreases with it; like a fish in little water, what joy is there? If one still drags mud and water along and sways three times at every step, then though one reads sutras and hears the Dharma day after day and understands a few lines of reasoning, what benefit is there? One must guard against the arising of the obstruction of the known, which is worse than the obstruction of afflictions. Pick up the pace and walk.

(Chen) Next, clarifying emptiness of substance in terms of the gift of Dharma. This has three parts: (Ji) first, clarifying that there is no dharma that can be spoken; next, clarifying that the hearer is empty of nature; third, clarifying that no dharma can be obtained.

After the supreme reward of merit, the text continues with the great section on the gift of Dharma precisely to show that all dharmas arise from conditions. For there must be the causes and conditions of giving and the six perfections before the facts and marks of the supreme reward of merit can occur. Hence the supreme reward of merit is spoken of in terms of fruit, that is, in terms of the dharmas produced. This section on the gift of Dharma speaks in terms of cause. Speaking in terms of cause is meant to show the meaning that arising from conditions is inexhaustible and cause and effect are endless. Why is this said? One should know that the moment one speaks of giving there are three sides: the giver, the recipient, and the thing given. Hence this great section on the gift of Dharma opens into three sections. The first section, clarifying that there is no dharma that can be spoken, speaks in terms of the giver; the next, clarifying that the hearer is empty of nature, speaks in terms of the recipient; and the third, clarifying that no dharma can be obtained, speaks in terms of the thing given. What the Buddha taught is always a speaking of what he realized; hence “no dharma can be obtained” speaks in terms of the dharma given. And as for the giver, how he comes to practice this giving and how he is able to practice it, his causes and conditions are utterly not one. And as for the recipient, how he comes to be a living being and how he is able to hear the Dharma, his causes and conditions are likewise very many. And as for what is given, how this thing comes to be and how it is obtained, the causes and conditions are again various. The causes and conditions on these three sides are already in thousands of differences and beyond describing; how much more so since, if the three sides do not gather together in one time and one place, this one matter of the Dharma-gift still cannot occur. How do they come to gather? Again they cannot without conditions. From this one may know that no matter is not born of causes and conditions.

Nor is this all. Since there is this one condition of the Dharma-gift, all kinds of fruits will in turn occur; fruits again become causes, and causes again become fruits. Fruit and cause, cause and fruit, from this onward are in thousands of differences and forever without end. It can be seen that the various facts and marks of the worldly and the world-transcending, what are called all dharmas, are nothing else at all but unbroken cause-and-effect and effect-and-cause, appearing and transforming in the minds and eyes of living beings. Living beings do not know how to contemplate deeply their purport, and so are deluded by these marks and point to them and name them: this dharma, that dharma. They fail to realize that what they point to as a cause is in fact the fruit of a preceding cause, and what they name a fruit is in truth the cause of a succeeding fruit. What are called cause-dharmas and fruit-dharmas have in themselves nothing fixed. Since nothing is fixed, nothing is real; and it is not merely that in an instant all becomes a thing of the past. Then to painstakingly discriminate and firmly cling, fixing this dharma as that dharma, is this not folly? Not only is one who takes the facts and marks to be truly existent foolish; one who takes the facts and marks to be truly non-existent is likewise foolish. Why? All dharmas are nothing but cause and effect and effect and cause, evolving in succession, dazzling the mind and eye, and cannot pause for even an instant. To cling to them as real, giving rise to one’s own bonds and losing one’s freedom, is folly beyond words. Yet although dharmas are not real, from beginningless time they arise whenever conditions meet; cause and effect and effect and cause continue instant by instant without ever breaking off. To cling stubbornly to emptiness and not know to accord with the principle of arising from conditions, to rely on supreme causes and conditions and attain supreme realization of fruit, means that one can neither realize the nature that is fundamentally not arising from conditions and stand beyond all dharmas arising from conditions so as to free oneself from the misery of bonds and gain the joy of freedom, nor make use of the facts and principle of arising from conditions to respond to faculties and accord with conditions, manifesting various dharmas to pull living beings out of suffering and give them joy. One who cannot transcend is bound to fall. Why? Because one has grasped emptiness wrongly. (One who, because he does not cling to true existence, also disbelieves in cause and effect, is said to grasp emptiness wrongly; this makes clear that he is bound to create evil.) Even if one does not grasp emptiness wrongly but merely leans toward emptiness, one may transcend arising from conditions but cannot make use of it, and so sinks into emptiness and stagnates in stillness, becoming a self-saver. (Such a one cultivates only a small cause and realizes only a small fruit, not knowing to rely on supreme causes and conditions and attain supreme realization of fruit. Hence though able to transcend and realize for himself the inherently possessed nature, he cannot make use of according with conditions to save living beings. The two vehicles are like this.) Hence the World-Honored One rebuked them: scorched sprouts and rotten seeds, fallen into the pit of the unconditioned. These two sicknesses of grasping emptiness, though their suffering and joy differ and their rising and sinking are far apart, are one in lacking wisdom.

The Buddha speaks this section to cause people to penetrate thoroughly the facts and principle of arising from conditions, so as to avoid the sickness of clinging to existence or to emptiness. And it causes those who have given rise to bodhi-mind and practice the bodhisattva path to penetrate the dharmas arising from conditions that are at once empty and provisional and at once provisional and empty, and to give broadly, so that self and others accord with this principle and cling to neither emptiness nor existence. Transcending the outward and yet attaining the center of the ring, one becomes a bodhisattva complete in compassion and wisdom. Why? By not clinging to existence, the self of persons is emptied; by not clinging to emptiness, the self of dharmas is emptied. With self and dharmas both emptied, one has the right prajñā-wisdom that penetrates the three emptinesses and realizes the prajñā-essence in which emptiness and existence are simultaneous. Becoming a Buddha is then not even difficult, let alone becoming a bodhisattva. Hence it says: if a bodhisattva penetrates no-self and no-dharma, the Tathāgata says he is truly called a bodhisattva.

From what has been said above, one may know that the three sides of giver, recipient, and gift, since they are all dharmas arising from conditions, are all empty in their very substance. Hence they are called the three wheels whose substance is empty. The three sides are figured as wheels because a wheel is a thing that turns without pause, and other things are crushed by the wheel and destroyed without remainder. This figures cause and effect and effect and cause changing and evolving in turn without ever resting, and also figures that the gift of wealth breaks stinginess and greed, the gift of fearlessness breaks misery and affliction, and the gift of Dharma can open right wisdom and break the three obstructions. What has been said above is all the essential purport of this section; explaining it first makes it easier to grasp when we enter the text.

blocks.text: Neither Dharma nor Spoken, Part Twenty-One

inline.s: (Ji) First, clarifying that there is no dharma that can be spoken. This has two parts: (Wu) first, speaking in accordance with faculties; next, fundamentally nothing to speak. (Wu) The first again has two: (Wei) first, showing that in speaking the Dharma there is no thought; next, explaining that to have thought is to cling.
(Wei) First, showing that in speaking the Dharma there is no thought.
["Subhūti, do not say that the Tathāgata thinks, ‘I should speak some dharma.’ Do not entertain this thought.

The several sections that follow have a profound and hidden purport. They are deep and concealed and not easy to see. Moreover the surface is making clear the meaning of the Tathāgata’s speaking the Dharma, while the core is teaching bodhisattvas how they should transcend thought. This is what is called speaking of this while intending that. Let me first explain the surface meaning layer by layer, and then speak of the intent within the words.

The first occurrence of the word “thought” is spoken from the side of the Tathāgata, as the text itself makes clear. The word “thought” in “do not entertain this thought” is spoken from the side of the elder, meaning that you should not entertain this thought. This word “thought” follows from the word “say” above. To say is to speak. To make this statement comes about because one has entertained this thought, and so he warns him not to entertain this thought. Where is the fault in entertaining this thought and making this statement? It lies in the four words “that I should.” And to entertain this thought and make this statement is to slander the Buddha. Hence the warning not to entertain such a thought or statement. What principle is this? The passage below under “why” precisely makes the reason clear, and one should examine it in detail below.
(Wei) Next, explaining that to have thought is to cling.
["Why? If a person says that the Tathāgata speaks some dharma, he slanders the Buddha and cannot understand what I have spoken.

“Why” asks why one should not entertain this thought or make this statement. “Speaks some dharma” means that in the mind there remains some dharma that is spoken, which is the meaning of entertaining the thought “I should.” Once this is said, the offense is very great and one must fall into the uninterrupted hell. Why? Because one thereby slanders the Buddha. This is why one should not entertain this thought or make this statement. Why is it slandering the Buddha? The sutra text seems not to say plainly, but in fact it has already hinted at it within the two words “Tathāgata.” Only one who has perfectly realized the inherent nature is called Tathāgata. In the empty and still nature, how could there be thought? How could there be a self? It is only ordinary beings whose deluded thoughts are not yet stilled and whose clinging to self is not yet emptied who entertain the thought “I should do such and such.” To say that the Tathāgata is like this is to see the Tathāgata as an ordinary being. Is that not slander? One should know that the one who speaks the Dharma is the reward and transformation Buddha, not the dharma body Tathāgata; yet one must realize the dharma body before becoming the reward and transformation body. Hence the reward and transformation body and the dharma body, though not one, are not different. Hence the dharma body is without thought and without speech, while the reward and transformation body, though it speaks, in truth has no thought. The sutra text specifically raises the Tathāgata to make this clear, showing that one must by no means doubt that the Buddha has the thought of speaking the Dharma. To have this doubt is no different from doubting that the Buddha-nature is empty and still and that he has not realized the dharma body; it is also no different from saying he has not yet become a Buddha. Hence it says that one thereby slanders the Buddha.

Further, the Buddha’s speaking of the Dharma is always a response to faculties. Faculty means the opportunity. Words that respond to faculties precisely make clear that speaking the Dharma too arises from conditions. Arising from conditions is empty in substance, and so the Dharma is fundamentally no Dharma. The Tathāgata has already realized emptiness of substance, and so to speak is to have not spoken. How could it be said that he speaks some dharma? How can the Buddha speak the Dharma according with conditions without giving rise to thought? It is by the power of the perfuming of compassionate vows when cultivating the cause, as said before. This principle is set out most clearly in the ten-fascicle Golden Light Sūtra, and must not go unknown. Let me cite and explain it. That sutra says: “The Buddha does not have this thought, ‘I now expound the twelve divisions of the teachings for the benefit of sentient beings.’” The twelve divisions of the teachings means the three baskets; the three baskets are opened out in detail into twelve parts. This says that the Buddha’s teaching of the sutras, vinaya, and treatises for the benefit of living beings never begins with the thought “I should do so.” The sutra also says: “Yet by the power of the roots of goodness and compassion from former times, toward those sentient beings, in accordance with their faculties, their inclinations, and their resolute understanding, without giving rise to discrimination, he spontaneously saves and ferries them, revealing, teaching, benefiting, and delighting them, to the end of the future without exhaustion.” This says that although he does not give rise to the thought “I should speak the Dharma to save living beings,” he can speak in accordance with those living beings’ faculties, what their minds delight in, and what they understand. And although he thus skillfully responds to opportunities and, to the end of the future, reveals, teaches, transforms, benefits all, delights all, and speaks the Dharma without end, still he has no thought discriminating among the opportunities; it is to be without discrimination and yet naturally perfectly accordant, which is what is called spontaneous. Why can he be like this? Because in former times, in the causal stage, his compassionate vows were fulfilled and he deeply contemplated arising from conditions, and the perfuming became a seed (roots of goodness), and the power of this brings it about. Yet when cultivating the cause, one should on the one hand contemplate the provisional existence of arising from conditions and on the other hand contemplate the inherently possessed true emptiness. (In this sutra’s section on opening right knowledge, the mind’s activity being unobtainable is spoken first, which is to cause one to contemplate true emptiness; then all dharmas arising from conditions is spoken, which is to cause one to contemplate provisional existence.) If one has not realized the nature of true emptiness, then even with fulfilled compassionate vows and deep contemplation of arising from conditions, one cannot manifest according with conditions. Hence the sutra also says: “Relying on the thusness of dharmas and on thusness-wisdom, one can attain freely and successfully in matters benefiting self and others. Relying on the thusness of dharmas and on thusness-wisdom, one speaks all kinds of Buddhadharma and even the dharmas of the hearers.” This says that only after realizing the nature are the two wisdoms accomplished. Relying on these two wisdoms, all matters benefiting both self and others are freely and successfully attained, and not only can one freely speak all kinds of dharma. There is no need to give rise to thought or discrimination; it is accomplished naturally, and this is freedom. The thusness of dharmas: dharma means the nature of dharmas, thus means true suchness, and the second “thus” means one thusness; it means being one thusness with the nature of dharmas and true suchness. This is another name for fundamental wisdom. Thusness-wisdom: the first “thus” means one thusness, the second “thus” means true suchness, and wisdom means fundamental wisdom; it means being one thusness with true suchness and fundamental wisdom. This is another name for subsequent wisdom.

Fundamental wisdom is the essence of the nature, while subsequent wisdom is the function of the nature. Only after attaining the essence can one give rise to function, and so other sutras translate it as subsequent wisdom. Because it is named in contrast to the subsequent to make the fundamental clear, it is also called wisdom, though in fact it is only the essence of the nature. Hence this sutra translates it as the thusness of dharmas and does not call it wisdom. Each has its own meaning, and neither is inadmissible. For fundamental wisdom speaks of its illuminating the true, and subsequent wisdom of its illuminating the conventional. Illuminating the true, it is only the one empty and still light of the nature, and it is acceptable not to call it wisdom; yet since the light of the nature shines brightly, calling it wisdom is also acceptable. Illuminating the conventional, it discerns the facts and marks in their thousands of differences, and it is fitting to call it wisdom; yet although it is called discernment, it does not give rise to thought or discrimination, and so it is called thusness-wisdom. The sutra further uses a simile to reveal this principle: “Just as immeasurable and boundless water-mirrors, relying on light, cause empty reflections to manifest all kinds of different marks, and the empty is precisely without marks.” Water and mirror both figure the nature; water figures purity and the mirror perfection. Immeasurable and boundless figures the nature pervading empty space and encompassing the dharma-realm. Light figures the two wisdoms, since wisdom has the meaning of brightness. Empty figures the empty and still essence of the nature. Reflection figures deluded thought. Different marks figure the marks of differentiated facts. Without marks figures no thought. The phrase “the empty is precisely without marks” precisely makes clear the meaning of the empty reflection, and shows that although all kinds of marks are manifested, within them there is still no mark, and so it is called empty. In sum, it says that the water-mirror being free of dust emits light; relying on this light, it can manifest all kinds of marks within the empty and dustless. The Buddha-nature is likewise: being without thought and empty and still, the light of wisdom is perfect and all-pervading. Relying on this light of wisdom, all kinds of matters are freely and successfully attained within the empty, still, and thoughtless. It can be seen that free and successful attainment is precisely brought about by the light of wisdom manifesting from no-thought and empty stillness.

Now to say that the Tathāgata entertains the thought “I should speak the Dharma” makes him the same as an ordinary being; how could he be the Tathāgata? And since he is not empty and still, how could he speak the Dharma freely? This is precisely what is called measuring the ocean of perfect enlightenment with the view of revolution, which is nowhere admissible. One should know that the speaking of the Dharma is like an echo in a valley, meaning that as a sound is carried through an empty valley, it responds whenever there is a stimulus, with no room for deliberate intent. It is also like the response of a drum to a mallet: a great stroke gives a great sound, a small stroke a small sound, exactly according to its measure, naturally and of itself. The Buddha’s speaking of the Dharma is just so. This is why one should not entertain this thought or statement. But then why does one entertain it? The World-Honored One traces the reason: for no other cause than that one cannot understand what I have spoken.

Someone may say: earlier the World-Honored One asked whether the Tathāgata speaks any dharma, and the elder plainly answered that the Tathāgata speaks nothing. Why then does the text here admonish the elder that he should not entertain the thought that the Tathāgata speaks some dharma, and say that he does not understand what is spoken? What is it that he does not understand? One should know that the elder is the fitting recipient, and that the words addressed to the elder are meant to admonish the whole assembly. See how it first says “do not say” and then says “if a person says”; how does it ever single out the elder? As for what he does not understand: in terms of this sutra, it guards against his hearing the earlier teachings that there is no fixed dharma for the Tathāgata to speak and that bodhisattvas, for the benefit of all living beings, should give in this way, and failing to understand them perfectly. Then he is bound to misunderstand the statement that the Tathāgata speaks nothing, and the other teachings too he will be unable to connect. He will say: bodhisattvas should still benefit living beings by giving, so how much more the Buddha, who appeared in the world precisely to speak the Dharma for the benefit of living beings; and now he is blazingly speaking this Diamond Prajñā. So the statement that the Tathāgata speaks nothing must mean that once spoken it is done, leaving not the slightest trace. Did it not say before that there is no fixed dharma for the Tathāgata to speak? One may know that it means only that there is no fixed dharma to speak, not that he speaks nothing at all; once spoken, it is not spoken, but at the very time of speaking, how could there be nothing spoken? To speak some dharma, though it is not without thought, yet all other thoughts may be transcended; if the thought of speaking the Dharma were transcended, how could one save living beings? And if one does not save living beings, how could one be called a Buddha? This is why they openly say that the Tathāgata entertains the thought “I should speak some dharma,” not knowing that this is slandering the Buddha. Ordinary beings’ views are often like this, and they fail to realize that it is precisely the opposite of the Buddhadharma. From this one may see how great a matter understanding is. Because of not understanding, one falls into wrong knowledge and wrong views, and by giving rise to doubt one harms oneself; and then one makes this statement and destroys others’ faith. Harming the Dharma and harming people is why one slanders the Buddha and the offense reaches to the uninterrupted hell. How does one know that what he does not understand lies here? From what is said below, which precisely applies a painful needle to the place where he does not understand in order to make him open up in understanding; hence one knows it.
(Wu) Next, fundamentally nothing to speak.
["Subhūti, one who speaks the Dharma has no dharma that can be spoken; therefore he is called one who speaks the Dharma."]

No dharma that can be spoken means to reveal that fundamentally there is nothing to speak. Why is there fundamentally nothing to speak? Because fundamentally there is no dharma. Since fundamentally there is no dharma, how could there be anything to speak? Hence it says there is no dharma that can be spoken. Why? Because no dharma is not arising from conditions. It was said before that there is no fixed dharma for the Tathāgata to speak, which precisely makes clear that fundamentally there is no dharma, and that only because conditions gather does a false and illusory mark appear, and so there is nothing fixed. But not knowing how to understand this thoroughly in terms of arising from conditions, one gives rise to all kinds of misunderstandings, and that is a mistake.
